LayerFS 

 Ephemeral Workspaces. Durable Shared History. 

 
 LayerFS is the substrate under your agents. Each one mounts a complete, writable
 Workspace over shared committed history, does its work, commits what it changed,
 and goes away.
 

 
 Get started ·
 Website ·
 Docs ·
 Benchmarks ·
 Video ·
 LayerFS × DSH ·
 Community

 layerfs v2 0 0 branch.
 Check there for the latest 2.0.0 work.

 

 Status: LayerFS 1.1.0,
 released as source: the JavaScript API split into @layerfs/agent , @layerfs/backend 
 and @layerfs/runtime under api/ , plus the layerfs command. It breaks
 code written for 1.0.0; see the release record.
 The results below are 1.0.0's, measured on main at e5c7aaae05 . The Store runs in its Disposable profile only, with no
 crash or power-loss durability: use LayerFS for agent work and its history, not
 as the only copy of data you cannot rebuild.

Since 1.1.0, LayerFS also supports native Windows dsh Live through WSL2 and its own Linux Docker Engine; see the Windows setup.

 
 Try it with LayerFS × DSH

 
 
 

LayerFS runs today through LayerFS × DSH , the dsh-layerfs plugin for
DeepSeek Harness. Agents in a dsh
session fork Branches, test them in Sandboxes, merge and publish, and the Work and
 History tabs show every agent's Branch, live.

 
 
 

 Core ideas

 
 
 
 
 01 · Ephemeral Computing 
 Compute exists only while a command runs.
 
 
 
 02 · Decentralized Agents 
 Agents on different computers share one serverless Store.
 
 
 
 03 · Multiagent Coordination 
 One project, many Branches. One Branch, many agents.
 
 
 
 
 
 04 · Recursive Filesystem 
 Fork recursively any Commit, at any depth.
 
 
 
 05 · Ultra Storage Optimization 
 157 snapshots of a real project in 100 MB, 19.9× smaller than Btrfs + zstd.
 
 
 
 06 · Instant Bootstrap 
 Dependencies come with every mount. No time lost reinstalling.
 
 
 

 And underneath them 

 Supporting idea In one line 
 --- --- --- 
 07 · Auto Checkpoints Every step an agent takes is a checkpoint to return to. 
 08 · Append-only Objects Saved objects are never rewritten. The Store only grows. 
 09 · Conflict Rules ( .lww ) Name the files that should never conflict. The newest edit wins. 
 10 · Big File, Small Edit An edit costs the size of the edit, not the size of the file. 

 See it run

 
 
 
 Agents fork Branches, work in Workspaces inside Sandboxes, commit, merge and publish to main . The history grows as they go. 

 Results

Every suite ran once on main at e5c7aaae05 through the JavaScript SDK. Each
row links to its method, environment and receipts.

 Suite What it measures LayerFS 1.0.0 
 --- --- --- 
 fs-bench Cloudflare Computer's own twelve-scenario filesystem benchmark, unchanged, same image 5.20 s vs 8.88 s, 1.71× faster ; faster in 10 of 12 scenarios 
 dsh-dedup A real project's history, 157 snapshots (4.94 GB of trees), kept as mountable Commits 100.1 MB vs 1,994.6 MB, 19.9× smaller than Btrfs + zstd; 156/156 read back 
 pjdfstest POSIX conformance, 8,798 assertions, against kernel overlayfs 0 unexpected failures ; keeps 76% of overlayfs's passes, every other failure a deliberate format limit 
 fsx Random reads, writes, mapped I/O and truncates, every byte checked 14/14 pass , 3.06 M ops, 0 miscompares 
 fsstress Four concurrent processes, then Commit, remount and compare 3,755/3,755 entries identical ; 5.21 GB captured by one Commit in 4.9 s 
 smallfile 100,000 files of 4 KiB, four threads, against libfuse passthrough Faster in 9 of 9 operations , 1.27×–10.71× 
 mdtest Metadata create, rename and remove, against libfuse passthrough 0.86–1.28× with 1 process, 1.21–4.22× with 4 
 fio Data I/O bandwidth, against libfuse passthrough Random read/write mixes 1.49–2.23×; slower on sequential write (0.31×), sequential read (0.81×) and random write (0.40×) 

 One sample per case, seed 1, no best-of. Host: arm64 Mac, Docker Desktop
linux/arm64, 8 CPUs, 8.3 GB; host load is recorded per suite. These are release
measurements, not a guarantee for your workload. Earlier fs-bench-pro results:
v0.1.4 ·
v0.1.5 ·
v0.1.6. 

 How it works

 

- Store. One SQLite file holds every Branch, Commit and content object. Each
 daemon and SDK process opens it directly; there is no database server.
- Branch, Commit, Layer. A Branch is a writable line of Commits. Publishing a
 Branch to main adds a Layer. Content is chunked and stored once.
- Workspace. A mount binds the whole committed tree without copying it. Writes
 go to the Workspace's own overlay until a Commit saves them. Unmount deletes
 the overlay, never history.
- Conflict. Two Commits that change the same file are refused with
 Conflict , unless a .lww rule says the newest edit wins. Publishing a
 stale Branch is different: it may skip newer main Layers; merge main into
 the Branch first (publish semantics).

 Prior art

LayerFS builds on well-known ideas: layered and union filesystems, copy-on-write
snapshots, content-addressed storage and throwaway execution environments. What
it adds is putting them together for agents: every tool call gets a full
writable tree, and every result becomes a Commit on a Branch in one shared Store.

 Prior work What it shares with LayerFS Where LayerFS differs 
 --- --- --- 
 overlayfs, UnionFS, container image layers A read-only lower tree with a writable upper layer, which is also where the "layer" name comes from The upper layer is not just thrown away or kept as a directory: Commit turns it into an immutable snapshot on a Branch, with history, merge and Conflict . overlayfs is in the kernel and more complete; LayerFS's FUSE view deliberately omits FIFOs, sockets, device nodes, set-id bits and separate atime/ctime (pjdfstest) 
 Btrfs and ZFS snapshots, reflinks Cheap copy-on-write snapshots that share unchanged data Sharing is by content, not by extent, so a file that is rewritten in full still stores only its new chunks. On a small-file history of 157 snapshots that gives 19.9
